findings.source_passage: Horrible old man! Who's over him, he cries;—aye, he would be a democrat to all above; look, how he lords it over all below!
findings.source_locator: paragraph 1, after 'tows me with a cable I have no knife to cut'
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is critically significant — Starbuck's characterization of Ahab as a 'democrat to all above' who 'lords it over all below' is a key interpretive moment for readings of Ahab's politics, authority, and class dynamics in the novel. Its complete absence removes interpretive weight the critical tradition depends on.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'Horrible old man! Who's over him, he cries;—aye, he would be a democrat to all above; look, how he lords it over all below!' verbatim or near-verbatim between the cable line and 'Yet is there hope.'

findings.source_passage: Oh! I plainly see my miserable office,—to obey, rebelling; and worse yet, to hate with touch of pity!
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of the most critically cited lines in the chapter — 'to obey, rebelling; and worse yet, to hate with touch of pity' defines Starbuck's tragic condition and is an interpretive keystone for his entire characterization across the novel. Its complete omission is a severe signature failure.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'I plainly see my miserable office,—to obey, rebelling; and worse yet, to hate with touch of pity!' verbatim in the draft.

findings.source_passage: my whole clock's run down; my heart the all-controlling weight, I have no key to lift again.
findings.source_locator: end of paragraph 1, after 'I would up heart, were it not like lead'
findings.why_it_matters: This closing image of the first paragraph — the clock metaphor — is prosodically distinctive and thematically resonant, crystallizing Starbuck's paralysis. 'I have no key to lift again' is a memorable period to the monologue's first movement and is absent entirely from the draft.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'my whole clock's run down; my heart the all-controlling weight, I have no key to lift again' at the close of the first paragraph.

findings.source_passage: Oh, God! to sail with such a heathen crew that have small touch of human mothers in them! Whelped somewhere by the sharkish sea.
findings.source_locator: paragraph 2, opening after the stage direction
findings.why_it_matters: The exclamation 'Whelped somewhere by the sharkish sea' is a voice-defining, rhetorically distinctive line; its rhythm and imagery mark Starbuck's register. The draft jumps immediately to 'Hark the infernal orgies,' cutting this voice-establishing opening entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the opening lament about the heathen crew and 'whelped somewhere by the sharkish sea' before the 'Hark' line.

findings.source_passage: Stand by me, hold me, bind me, O ye blessed influences!
findings.why_it_matters: The final plea — 'Stand by me, hold me, bind me, O ye blessed influences!' — is the rhetorical and emotional climax of the entire monologue, a prayer-like incantation that closes the chapter on a note of desperate supplication. Its omission flattens the ending catastrophically.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'Stand by me, hold me, bind me, O ye blessed influences!' as the final line of the draft.

findings.source_passage: 'tis in an hour like this, with soul beat down and held to knowledge,—as wild, untutored things are forced to feed—Oh, life! 'tis now that I do feel the latent horror in thee! but 'tis not me! that horror's out of me!
findings.why_it_matters: The draft collapses the doubled 'Oh, life!' apostrophe and the archaic contraction 'tis,' the simile of 'wild, untutored things forced to feed,' and the emphatic 'that horror's out of me!' — all of which are rhythmically and rhetorically distinctive. Only a bare paraphrase survives.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'Oh, life! 'tis in an hour like this' passage with its doubled invocation and the simile intact; at minimum preserve 'but 'tis not me! that horror's out of me!'

summary: The draft drops three high-severity signature passages — the 'democrat to all above' characterization of Ahab, the 'miserable office—to obey, rebelling' line, and the 'clock's run down' closing image — along with two medium-severity voice erasures (the 'whelped by the sharkish sea' opening and the 'Stand by me, bind me' climax), gutting both interpretive weight and rhetorical power from Starbuck's soliloquy.
